question_text: Draw the output capacitor current and voltage waveforms alongside the inductor current. Why do they look like this?
answer_text: The capacitor current is an AC triangle wave centered perfectly at 0A. The capacitor voltage is a smooth DC line with tiny parabolic ripples.
explanation_text: The inductor provides a DC current with an AC triangle ripple riding on top of it. The load consumes the flat DC portion. By KCL (I_cap = I_L - I_load), the capacitor is forced to absorb only the AC triangle ripple, meaning its current matches the inductor's AC ripple but centered around 0A. Because V = (1/C) * integral(I dt), integrating this triangle current creates a sequence of tiny parabolas (the voltage ripple).
bonus_question_text: When does the output voltage reach its absolute maximum peak during the switching cycle?
bonus_answer_text: Right in the middle of the OFF state, exactly when the capacitor current crosses 0A going downward (finishing its charging phase).
